articles.summary_snippet: Unfolding crisis shows importance of ‘human connections’ over the long term – especially in under-vaccinated areas Tristan Sharratt, a family nurse practitioner and public health researcher, began serving an Amish community in central New York almost inadvertently. A friend told an Amish neighbor that Sharratt was accepting new patients and was a good, solid guy. Word spread quickly, and now Sharratt sees many members of the community, which numbers in the hundreds. He is what is called a “trusted messenger” – someone who understands a community and has earned their respect. Other trusted messengers can be neighbors, co-workers, customers, midwives, or people who work as long-distance drivers for the Amish. Connecting with such people will be crucial for ending the measles outbreak and preventing future crises. Continue reading...

articles.title: The life, death and improbable rebirth of LA’s most beloved diner
articles.summary_snippet: For decades, it served pancakes, hash browns and steaks to hungry Angelenos. Then came closure, and a city mourned – but now the Original Pantry is back Sometimes, an old-school American diner is just a diner. And sometimes, like the Original Pantry in downtown Los Angeles, it feels like the heart and soul of a city, a bellwether of good times and bad. For decades it was famous for never closing. Located in a low-slung shotgun building on a busy corner, it fed politicians, movie stars, students, criminals and street bums around the clock, seven days a week. The doors had no locks, because the place had no need for them. The portions were huge, the prices dirt cheap, and many of the servers, in bow ties and white shirts, looked like extras from a Harold Lloyd two-reeler. Continue reading...

articles.summary_snippet: I believe human judgment remains essential Last year, I nearly quit mathematics. On 20 November, Levent Alpöge announced that, working with Claude, he had proved the Riemann hypothesis, a 167-year-old problem about the distribution of prime numbers. The Lean and Mathlib communities have since certified the formal proof. We are only beginning to understand the argument. What kind of future awaits someone beginning a life in mathematics? In May 2025, I led the number theory team for Epoch AI’s FrontierMath project. We wrote difficult problems to test large language models. I watched an unreleased ChatGPT model compute all the moments of Tamagawa numbers of elliptic curves, drawing on work by Manjul Bhargava and Roger Heath-Brown, and on papers my father wrote in the 1960s. The danger is that the two strongmen ultimately reap the benefits On the facade of Stenbock House, the Estonian prime minister’s neoclassical office building on a hill in Tallinn, sits a plaque commemorating the murder of 10 heads of government. They were all killed by Soviet forces after the USSR’s invasion of Estonia in 1940. For 51 years, Estonia was occupied by its imperial neighbour; for the past 25 years it has lived independently in its shadow. For the politicians and government officials who work at Stenbock House, the plaque is a constant reminder of the risk the small Baltic nation (population 1.4 million) faces from a neighbour 100 times its size. Created in a Rio de Janeiro prison in the 1970s as a self-protection group for prisoners, it started out with low-level crimes like muggings and bank robberies. But in the 1980s, the group moved into the cocaine trade, working with Colombian drug cartels and taking on a social leadership role in many of Rio’s marginalized neighborhoods.
